summary.oneLiner: Sarla Performance Fibers is a Silvassa-headquartered specialty synthetic yarn maker and India's sole manufacturer of Nylon 66 and only producer of pure nylon, exporting to more than 62 countries.
summary.business: Sarla manufactures a comprehensive range of synthetic yarns and threads - polyester and nylon textured yarns, twisted yarns, dyed yarns, covered yarns, high-tenacity yarns, barre-free nylon yarns and application-specific sewing threads - from state-of-the-art units in Silvassa, Vapi and Dadra built on over three decades of industry expertise. The company has shifted deliberately from commodity apparel yarn toward high-tenacity nylon and polyester and specialty yarns serving sportswear, military, industrial sewing thread, automotive, medical and home-textile applications, with value-added products now approximately 50% of the product portfolio. It supplies leading global brands both directly and through intermediary networks, and describes itself as the most vertically integrated textured sewing thread manufacturer in India.

Nylon yarns: High-tenacity Nylon 6 and Nylon 66 industrial yarn
Covered and dyed yarns: High-Tenacity Covered Dyed Yarns and Threads

Medical textile products for implants, catheters and orthopedic applications

currentContext.expansion:
Sarla is headquartered in Mumbai and runs state-of-the-art manufacturing facilities in Silvassa, Dadra and Vapi, roughly 160 km north of Mumbai. The principal units in Silvassa, supported by an auxiliary facility in Dadra about 10 km away, are vertically integrated to cover the entire value chain from spinning through to advanced high-bulk and high-stretch processing, with in-house bonding and kings pool winding enabling over 250 value-added yarns and threads and customised orders ranging from a few hundred to several thousand kilograms. The company states it holds India's largest capacity in air covering as well as in single and double conventional covering. Its dyeing facility in Vapi, inside the Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation zone, processes all fibre types from stretch nylon to high-tenacity yarns and textured sewing threads, with a Colour Bank of over 5,000 shades, an in-house lab developing an average of 8 new colours daily and automated dyeing supporting batch sizes from 1 kg to 500 kg. All facilities are ISO 9001:2015 certified and average machine age is under five years, among the lowest in the industry.

On the current investment cycle, management states that during the year Sarla invested INR 4.8 crore in plant and machinery additions and modernization, primarily towards technology upgrades, supplementing nearly INR 125 crore invested over the preceding six years in building future-ready manufacturing capabilities. Looking ahead, approximately INR 20 crore has been earmarked towards modernization, automation, and selective capacity expansion. Sarla says it continues to scale up its Nylon 6 and Nylon 66 capacities in response to sustained and rising demand, and that expansion is guided by strong order visibility, with the company progressing toward swift capacity utilization to translate into higher sales volumes, improved price realizations and better margins. A SAP rollout has added granular machine-level data on breakdowns, spare parts and replacements, cutting yarn breakage and raising machine speeds, product quality and machine uptime.

The milestones timeline records the historical build-out: the original 100% Export Oriented Unit as Sarla Polyester Private Limited, an in-house dyeing plant in Vapi, a second manufacturing unit in Silvassa, a thread manufacturing unit at Silvassa's Amli Piparia Industrial Area for polyester textured yarn, a spinning plant converting nylon chips into high-tenacity Nylon 6 and Nylon 66 industrial yarn, a large expansion of the dyeing plant, commencement of Nylon 66 high-tenacity yarn manufacture as a niche product in India, a new plant commissioned in Dadra, GODET technology machinery for barre-free yarn described as a first in India, entry into wind power with a 1.25 MW wind turbine generator in Gujarat followed by 5 new windmills of 7.5 MW capacity, and overseas footprint additions including Sarla Europe LDA in Portugal, Sarla Flex LLC in South Carolina USA and the Savitex S.A. de C.V. venture. No rupee capex quantum is disclosed under a named capital-commitments or segment-capital-expenditure block in this bundle.

Management states that Sarla's expansion is guided by strong order visibility, and that US tariff-related uncertainty impacted order flows during the second half of FY 2025-26, with an expected recovery in demand across key export markets underpinning the FY 2026-27 outlook.

risks.risk: Qualified audit opinion - regulatory approvals still awaited on the Sarla Flex Inc. preference share sale
risks.note: The auditors issued a Qualified Opinion on both the standalone and consolidated financial statements, drawing attention to Notes 53 and 54 on Exceptional Items, where the Company recognised a loss on the sale of 1% Non-Cumulative Redeemable Preference Shares held in its wholly owned subsidiary Sarla Flex Inc. The Company has applied for the necessary regulatory approvals for the sale, the write-off of the loss, and the subsequent receipt of sale proceeds, and those approvals were still awaited as at the date of the audit report - leaving both the accounting treatment and the recovery of proceeds unresolved.

risks.risk: Export concentration and US tariff exposure
risks.note: Export revenue rose to 60.5% of total sales in FY26 from 55.7% in FY25, so trade policy is a first-order earnings variable. After the April 2025 US reciprocal tariff announcement, an additional 25% penalty tariff was layered on India in August 2025 over Russian oil purchases, taking total duties to 50% and erasing India's brief cost advantage against Bangladesh and Vietnam. Management attributes the FY26 revenue decline of 6% to temporary demand softness from US tariff-related uncertainty which hit order flows in the second half.

risks.risk: Crude oil and petrochemical feedstock cost volatility
risks.note: As a synthetic yarn converter, Sarla's input costs track polyester and nylon feedstock. Crude averaged around USD 69 per barrel for much of FY26 but surged toward USD 120 per barrel in the closing weeks, directly pressuring feedstock costs for synthetic fibre manufacturers. Management cites raw material price volatility and elevated energy costs as a driver of the FY26 EBITDA margin decline, and flags input cost pressure as capable of constraining the margin recovery expected in FY 2026-27.

Disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the ongoing Middle East conflict elevated freight and insurance costs through the closing months of the year and complicated supply-chain logistics, adding uncertainty specifically to Gulf-region exports. For an exporter shipping to more than 62 countries, freight cost volatility is a persistent margin and service-level risk; management names it alongside crude as the most significant near-term risk.

risks.risk: Foreign exchange exposure on foreign-currency borrowings and multi-currency revenue
risks.note: Standalone EBITDA margin fell to 14% from 19%, a decline management says was significantly influenced by a one-time foreign exchange loss on Euro-denominated borrowings; excluding it, margin would have been approximately 19%. With over 60% of sales exported and borrowings held in foreign currency, currency volatility flows straight to reported profitability.

risks.risk: Consumer preference shift toward natural and organic fibres
risks.note: Explicitly flagged in the Board's report: rising consumer inclination toward natural alternatives could gradually erode synthetic yarn market share. Sarla's entire portfolio is polyester and nylon based, so a durable substitution away from man-made fibre would strike the core business.

Explicitly flagged in the Board's report: advancements in alternative materials could challenge existing product relevance and require continuous adaptation. This is a live threat given the company's competitive position rests on specific engineered products such as barre-free nylon, high-tenacity yarns and covered yarns.

risks.risk: Working-capital strain from relaxed credit terms and deliberate inventory build-up
risks.note: Debtors turnover moderated from 4.58x to 3.90x owing to a strategic relaxation of credit terms extended to customers to support relationships and volume momentum, while inventory turnover fell from 5.35x to 4.80x on a deliberate inventory build-up in response to geopolitical supply-chain disruption. Both decisions lengthen the cash cycle and raise counterparty and inventory-value exposure if demand stays soft.

risks.risk: Volume decline and demand cyclicality in a commodity-adjacent end market
risks.note: Sales volumes fell 10.63%, from 13.73 lakh tons to 11.53 lakh tons, partially offset by improved realisations. Demand is tied to global apparel and home-textile order flows, which the report describes as subject to irregular demand cycles, political instability in Bangladesh reshaping order patterns, and moderating global growth of about 3.3% in 2026.

risks.risk: Unconsolidated joint ventures with financials unavailable since FY 2021-22
risks.note: The three joint ventures - Sarla Tekstil Filament Sanayi Ve Tic. (Turkey, 45%), MRK S.A. De C.V. (Mexico, 33.33%) and Savitex S.A. De C.V. (40%) - are carried at cost and excluded from consolidation because updated audited financial statements for years after FY 2021-22 have not been made available despite management's continued efforts. The Board has confirmed no additional impairment is warranted on available information, but the carrying values rest on four-year-old accounts.

themes.title: Textiles - apparel/home-textile exports + synthetics
themes.need: India textiles ride three tailwinds at once: China+1 sourcing shifts, the India-UK FTA (signed) + India-EU FTA (advancing), and US tariff normalization - favouring apparel exporters (GOKEX/PGIL/PDSL) and US-heavy home-textile names (WELSPUNLIV/HIMATSEIDE). A second leg = value-added synthetics/recycling (FILATEX, SANATHAN, CENTENKA, GANECOS) and cotton-yarn spread recovery (VTL/NITINSPIN/SPORTKING) plus branded apparel (PAGEIND, ARVIND, RAYMONDLSL).
themes.driver: FTA implementation + US-India trade-deal clarity; festive/wedding demand; cotton-yarn spread; anti-dumping rulings.
